Income and Life Expectancy Around the World

2020 comparisons, country exceptions, and historical change

Execution status: This is an independently checked preview, calculated and plotted in Python from the supplied CSV files. It is not an R-knitted report. The accompanying indicator_report.Rmd contains the full R analysis with github_document output, hidden code, inline R statistics, and all seven plots. An R runtime was unavailable in the authoring environment, and installation was blocked; R execution and the requested knit-review loop remain unverified. Run source("run_report.R") in R from the unzipped project folder to knit and validate the R output.

1. Data and research question

Question: How strongly is national average daily income associated with life expectancy in 2020, and what does that relationship leave unexplained?

This report uses only the two supplied indicator files for its numerical findings. lex.csv is life expectancy at birth, measured in years. mincpcap_cppp.csv is mean daily household income or consumption expenditure per person, adjusted for purchasing power and inflation. It is not annual GDP per capita, a salary, or median income. The current indicator metadata describes 2021 PPP international dollars; the uploads contain no version or PPP-base-year field. Therefore, the supplied values are kept unchanged and labeled PPP-adjusted international dollars per person per day, without asserting a verified base year.[1]

Each file has a country-code column (geo), a name column, and 301 year columns spanning 1800-2100. Future-year entries are not treated as observed outcomes. The main comparison uses 2020 only; the historical investigation uses 2000-2019, followed by a separate 2019-2020 comparison. Gapminder documents that its series can combine estimates, interpolation, and projections; the uploads do not identify which method produced each cell.[2][3]

Coverage and quality controls

Indicator Country rows Available in 2020 Mapped polygons
Life expectancy 194 194 166
Daily income / consumption 193 193 166

There are 193 complete country pairs in 2020. Liechtenstein appears in the life-expectancy file but not the income file and is excluded from paired statistics, not silently filled. Country codes, rather than row order or names, identify matches. Both 2020 columns are numeric and complete within their respective files, the country keys are unique, and all income values are positive. No indicator values are imputed, and no extreme observations are removed from the main analysis.

The low-resolution map omits 28 life-expectancy countries and 27 income countries, mainly small countries and island states. They remain in the indicator tables and, when paired, all statistics. Unfilled map areas mean no matched indicator value, not zero. The map is a general geographic reference, not a reconstruction of exact 2020 political boundaries.[4]

All summaries weight countries equally. They are not population-weighted world averages. Decimal places preserve supplied values; they do not imply that the underlying estimates are accurate to that precision.

2. The three highlighted countries

Country Life expectancy (years) Daily income (PPP-adjusted int$)
USA 77.1 96.5305
SPAIN 82.1 52.6164
GUINEA 61.1 6.8697

Spain’s life expectancy is 5.0 years higher than the USA’s, although its daily income is only 54.5% of the USA’s. Guinea is lower on both indicators. The USA’s income is 14.1 times Guinea’s, but that ratio is not a proportional measure of health and has no causal interpretation.

4. Relationship between income and life expectancy

Each dot represents one country. The horizontal axis is logarithmic, while labels show the original income amounts. The fitted line is the unweighted regression:

Fitted life expectancy = 56.158 + 4.032 x log2(daily income).

Comparison Correlation Model R-squared Leave-one-country-out RMSE (years)
Raw income versus life expectancy 0.480 0.230 9.33
Log2 income versus life expectancy 0.830 0.690 4.08
Spearman rank relationship 0.853 Not applicable Not applicable

Brief interpretation. Higher-income countries generally have longer life expectancy. The association is clearer for proportional income differences than for equal dollar differences: the log-income model has R-squared 0.690, compared with 0.230 for a straight raw-dollar model. In the log-income fit, a doubling of income is associated with 4.03 additional years of life expectancy. This describes differences between countries in 2020; it does not predict what would happen if a particular country’s income doubled.

The log fit is consistent with a curve that flattens per additional dollar, but that functional form remains a modeling choice. Its predictions should not be extrapolated outside the observed income range. The remaining variation, and the Spain-USA contrast, show that income is not a complete explanation. These two datasets cannot establish the roles of healthcare access, education, inequality, conflict, or other possible factors.

The leave-one-country-out error holds out each country in turn and summarizes the model’s prediction error in years. It is a sensitivity check, not an evaluation of future forecasting ability. No statistical-significance or causal-effect claims are made.

5. Deeper findings and questions

5.1. A few very high incomes distort the raw-dollar picture

The highest income is Monaco: 513.5429 int$/day. As a sensitivity check only, removing Monaco increases the raw-income correlation from 0.480 to 0.738. The log-income correlation changes much less, from 0.830 to 0.840. Monaco remains in the main analysis.

Further question: Does the apparent relationship depend on scale or an influential country? The rank-based Spearman correlation of 0.853 supports the positive ordering without using dollar distances. The raw-dollar model’s larger held-out error also highlights its sensitivity to very high-income observations.

5.2. Longevity rises across income groups, but income is not destiny

Income quartile Countries Income range (int/day)|Medianincome(int/day) Median life expectancy (years)
Q1: lowest 49 1.64-6.60 4.52 63.60
Q2 48 6.69-14.56 10.20 71.35
Q3 48 14.79-33.40 19.06 74.65
Q4: highest 48 33.94-513.54 60.11 81.10

These quartiles are defined from the 193 countries, not official income classifications. Median life expectancy rises from 63.60 years in the lowest-income quartile to 81.10 years in the highest. These are country medians, not medians across people, and they do not imply that every richer country outperforms every poorer country.

5.3. Which countries depart from the income-only expectation?

A residual is actual life expectancy minus the fitted value. Positive values mean longevity above the model’s expectation; negative values mean longevity below it. These are not health-system quality rankings.

Country Actual years Fitted years Actual minus fitted (years)
USA 77.1 82.74 -5.64
SPAIN 82.1 79.21 +2.89
GUINEA 61.1 67.37 -6.27

The USA is 5.64 years below the fitted value, Spain 2.89 years above, and Guinea 6.27 years below. The largest departures, including Monaco and North Korea in this supplied dataset, should prompt checks against country source notes rather than confident claims about performance. Measurement limitations, omitted factors, and model shape can all create residuals. The files do not include observation-level uncertainty flags.

Further question: Would these differences remain after adding inequality, age-specific mortality, education, and health-service measures? Those variables are not supplied, so the present report cannot distinguish those explanations.

5.4. Strong differences between countries do not imply strong links between changes

Across 193 countries from 2000 to 2019, the correlation between the log change in income and the change in life expectancy is only 0.089. This is far weaker than the association between income levels and longevity levels in 2020. The median country gained 4.4 years of life expectancy, and 187 countries improved. The median income increase was 44.1%.

Country Life expectancy, 2000 Life expectancy, 2019 Longevity gain (years) Income change (%)
USA 76.8 78.9 +2.1 +24.6
SPAIN 79.4 83.3 +3.9 +25.9
GUINEA 53.5 61.4 +7.9 +46.2

Guinea gained 7.9 years, more than Spain or the USA over this period. This does not demonstrate that income is unimportant: starting conditions, different timing, omitted factors, and measurement changes can weaken change-on-change relationships. It does show why a cross-country association should not be interpreted as a forecast for each country’s progress.

5.5. The 2020 change is not simply movement along the income curve

Between 2019 and 2020, life expectancy declined in 163 of 193 paired countries, while income declined in 130. Median country-level changes were -0.8 years and -2.3% income. In 52 countries, longevity fell even though the income indicator rose.

Country Life expectancy change (years) Income change (%)
USA -1.8 +2.55
SPAIN -1.2 +0.28
GUINEA -0.3 +2.07

All three highlighted countries fall in that last group. A positive household-income or consumption estimate is not evidence that GDP increased. These observations motivate questions about health and economic shock timing, income support, and how the series were constructed. They do not independently identify a pandemic effect or explain the opposite movements.

5.6. Large one-year income jumps warrant a source audit

There are 43 one-year income changes of at least 40% in absolute value in 2000-2020. This threshold is an exploratory flag, not a statistical test and not a rule for excluding data. Some changes may be real; others may reflect survey changes, splicing, or estimation. The files lack the metadata needed to decide.

Country Period Previous income (int/day)|Newincome(int/day) Change (%)
Bulgaria 2006-2007 12.2998 32.1106 +161.1
Latvia 2006-2007 20.8944 51.5463 +146.7
Russia 2013-2014 29.7692 71.8501 +141.4
Estonia 2002-2003 12.8455 29.8376 +132.3
Serbia 2017-2018 15.1162 35.0340 +131.8
Romania 2005-2006 9.0652 20.1893 +122.7

Further question: Would the longitudinal results remain similar after checking country survey documentation and using consistent source segments? These jumps are a reason for source verification, not automatic claims about economic transformation or grounds for silently deleting observations.

6. Conclusions and limitations

The central finding is a strong positive association between daily income and life expectancy in 2020, especially on a logarithmic income scale. But the Spain-USA contrast, large residuals, and weak link between 2000-2019 changes show that the cross-country income relationship is neither a causal law nor a complete account of health.

This is exploratory analysis of equally weighted country estimates. It cannot measure within-country inequality and has no observation-level uncertainty intervals or source flags. The uploads’ PPP base year cannot be certified from the files alone. Historical interpolation or splicing may affect trends. All future-year values are excluded. A more explanatory study would verify source consistency and add health, demographic, inequality, and education variables before making policy or causal claims.[2][3]

7. Reproducibility and sources

Numerical source: the user’s lex(1).csv and mincpcap_cppp(1).csv, preserved as data/lex.csv and data/mincpcap_cppp.csv. No replacement indicator values were downloaded. Results and omitted-country lists are included in results/.

Execution distinction: This preview was calculated with Python and converted to HTML with Pandoc. The accompanying Rmd independently implements the analysis in R and does not require Python. When run, it creates indicator_report.md, an HTML preview, seven charts in r_figures/, and tables in results_r/. The R runner then reads the actual Markdown and checks labels, plot references, hidden code, and agreement with the independent baseline for unchanged input files. Those R checks have not been executed here. The preview’s data checks, plots, and rendered Markdown were reviewed separately.

[1] Indicator definitions: Gapminder indicator metadata, entries lex and mincpcap_cppp. Current metadata interprets indicator names; it does not certify the uploads’ exact release.

[2] Source construction: Gapminder: Life Expectancy at Birth and Mean Household Income documentation.

[3] Data-quality caution: Gapminder documentation overview. Gapminder explains its gap-filling approach and cautions against interpreting broad visual estimates as precise measurements.

[4] Geography: Natural Earth, public-domain low-resolution country boundaries bundled from the local pyogrio test fixture. See reference/SOURCES.md for code repairs and map limitations. Population and GDP attributes in that boundary source were removed and are not used.

Rendering documentation: R Markdown GitHub document and render.
